title: 2 Chronicles 10:1–15
context: After Solomon’s death, all Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king. Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had fled from Solomon to Egypt, returns and joins the people in asking Rehoboam to lighten the heavy yoke Solomon had laid on them. Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the older advisers who had served his father, follows the harsh advice of the young men who grew up with him, and answers the people roughly. The Chronicler adds that “it was brought about by God,” so that the LORD might establish the word he spoke through Ahijah the Shilonite (10:15). The parallel is 1 Kings 12:1–15, which this account follows closely. Chronicles does not narrate Ahijah’s prophecy to Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:29–39), though it assumes readers know it. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about foolish leadership, God’s faithfulness to his word, and Rehoboam’s responsibility; how God’s purpose relates to human folly is treated at Judges 9:23, as in the notes on 1 Kings 12:15.

verses.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has gathered to make him king. Arminian readers note that the northern tribes come with real expectations and a real voice. The kingship is offered, but the people’s willingness to serve depends on how the new king responds to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the scene is set for the fulfillment of God’s word through Ahijah (10:15), though the participants do not know it yet. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the opening of a decisive moment, in which human choices and God’s purpose will meet at Shechem.

verses.text: When Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from the presence of King Solomon), Jeroboam returned out of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam, who had fled from Solomon to Egypt, hears the news and returns. Arminian readers note that he acts on his own initiative, ready to take part in what follows. 1 Kings 11:40 says he had fled to Shishak, the king who will later invade Judah (12:2).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see providence bringing back the man to whom God had promised ten tribes (1 Kings 11:31). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparing for the division, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 12:2, without assuming details of Jeroboam’s movements beyond what the text gives.

verses.text: They sent and called him; and Jeroboam and all Israel came, and they spoke to Rehoboam, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The people send for Jeroboam, and together with all Israel he speaks to Rehoboam. Arminian readers note that the people act collectively and choose their spokesman. The scene shows a community seeking a fair hearing from its new king before pledging its loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Jeroboam’s leading role and see the narrative moving toward the outcome God had announced. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a legitimate request brought by the people, and neither treats the assembly itself as rebellion.

verses.text: “Your father made our yoke grievous. Now therefore make the grievous service of your father and his heavy yoke which he put on us, lighter, and we will serve you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy yoke and grievous service his father imposed, promising to serve him if he does. Arminian readers note the reasonableness of the request. A king’s rule calls for justice and care, and the people’s loyalty is offered on fair terms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a just appeal, and they note that the burden of Solomon’s later reign is acknowledged here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reasonable plea for relief, which tests whether Rehoboam will rule as a servant of God and of the people.

verses.text: He said to them, “Come again to me after three days.” So the people departed.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam asks for three days before answering. Arminian readers note that the delay gives him time to seek counsel and make a wise decision. The pause shows that the outcome was not yet settled from the human side; Rehoboam had a real choice before him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a prudent step that could have led to a good outcome. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a moment of decision, with Rehoboam responsible for how he uses the three days, and neither finds a doctrinal question in the delay itself.

verses.text: King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, “What counsel do you give me about how to answer these people?”
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam consults the older men who had served Solomon. Arminian readers note that he has access to experienced counsel. Wisdom is available to him; the question is whether he will receive it. The verse sets up a choice between two kinds of advice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the value of seasoned counsel and the irony that Solomon’s son, heir to great wisdom, will reject it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as highlighting the importance of wise advisers and the responsibility of a leader to listen.

verses.text: They spoke to him, saying, “If you are kind to these people, please them, and speak good words to them, then they will be your servants forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: The older men advise kindness: please the people, speak good words, and they will be your servants forever. Arminian readers see the wisdom of servant leadership. A king who serves his people gains their loyalty; the advice offers a path to peace and unity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise commend the counsel as wise and godly, reflecting the ideal of a king who rules for the good of others. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as sound advice that Rehoboam was responsible to heed, and both see in it a lasting principle of leadership.

verses.text: But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam abandons the older men’s counsel and turns to the young men who grew up with him. Arminian readers see a real and culpable choice. He prefers advisers who share his outlook, and the narrative holds him responsible for rejecting wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see folly and responsibility in Rehoboam’s choice, which the narrator will also place within God’s purpose (10:15). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Rehoboam’s own decision, freely made and morally accountable, at the turning point of the story.

verses.text: He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may give an answer to these people, who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter’?”
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam asks the young men how to answer the people’s request to lighten the yoke. Arminian readers note that he frames the question as “we,” identifying with his peers. His choice of counselors already shapes the answer he will receive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the shift in Rehoboam’s alliances and the danger of seeking advice from those who will tell him what he wants to hear. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Rehoboam’s path toward folly, for which he remains responsible.

verses.text: The young men who had grown up with him spoke to him, saying, “Thus you shall tell the people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter on us;’ thus you shall say to them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.
verses.arminianNotes: The young men advise a harsh reply: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.” Arminian readers see arrogance in the counsel, which treats the people’s appeal as a challenge to be crushed. Pride, not wisdom, shapes their advice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the folly of answering a just plea with boasting. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of proud and foolish counsel, contrasting sharply with the older men’s advice, and both see in it a warning about the abuse of power.

verses.text: Now whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The young men continue: Rehoboam will add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions instead of whips. Arminian readers note the escalating threat, which shows contempt for the people. Such words invite the rebellion that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the harshness of the counsel and its disregard for the people’s burden. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of foolish advice and see in it the opposite of the servant leadership commended in 10:7.

verses.text: So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king asked, saying, “Come to me again the third day.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam and all the people return on the third day, as the king asked. Arminian readers note that the people keep their part of the arrangement, waiting for a fair answer. The responsibility now rests entirely with Rehoboam.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the people’s patience and the moment of decision that has arrived. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up Rehoboam’s answer, with the people having acted in good faith and the king about to choose his course.

verses.text: The king answered them roughly; and King Rehoboam abandoned the counsel of the old men,
verses.arminianNotes: The king answers roughly and abandons the counsel of the older men. Arminian readers see Rehoboam’s choice made final. His harshness is his own, and the narrator emphasizes that he had better counsel available and rejected it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a king acting foolishly and responsibly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Rehoboam’s decisive act of folly, which the next verses will show leading to the division of the kingdom.

verses.text: and spoke to them after the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam repeats the young men’s words: he will add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions. Arminian readers note that the king fully adopts the harsh counsel. His words expose a failure of wisdom and compassion that will cost him most of his kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king speaking in pride, rejecting the people’s just appeal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Rehoboam’s own responsible choice and as a sobering example of how a leader’s words can divide a nation.

verses.text: So the king didn’t listen to the people; for it was brought about by God, that the LORD might establish his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verses.arminianNotes: The king did not listen, “for it was brought about by God,” to establish the word spoken through Ahijah. Arminian readers see God directing Rehoboam’s freely chosen folly toward his announced purpose, without making God the author of the king’s pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God ordaining the outcome through Rehoboam’s responsible choice, so that his word through Ahijah stands. Shared ground: both traditions affirm God’s providence and Rehoboam’s guilt together; their difference on such texts is treated at Judges 9:23, as in the notes on 1 Kings 12:15.
